entry.title: How Will We Judge?
entry.content:
I hate that we have to judge theorists but departments need to make decisions about PhD admission, faculty hiring, tenure and promotion. Artificial intelligence adds new wrinkles to the process. AI makes it easier to prove theorems and write up papers, certainly leading to more papers. And how do we judge the role that an author plays in an AI-assisted or AI-generated paper? And are we rewarding good prompting and access to the pricier AI models?

These issues go back before the AI age. As our field has become more metric driven, we've seen a significant increase in the number of research papers from undergrads, grad students and young professors, often at the least publishable unit, just good enough to get accepted at various conferences. Bill told me about a quote he heard, "Deans can't read but they can count." Too often even our CS colleagues will count papers as well.

When I was department chair, I had faculty candidates upload a single paper with their submission. That gave us a single paper to read, though I'm not sure it always got read.

Since our papers list authors alphabetically instead of by contribution, we already had challenges sussing out the role an individual author played in the paper. With AI papers we often get an AI disclosure, but once we use that for judging a theorist, people will write those disclosures carefully, maybe in a misleading way or worse.

Here we could rely on recommendation letters. In computer science, letter writers tend to write the most positive letter without lying, so to read a letter properly you need to reverse that process. But now that many of these letters seem to be AI generated themselves, that muddles the information we get.

How do real companies deal with hiring? A company might wait until it gets a better feel for just what roles AI will play in research and teaching, but academic departments tend to fill slots because they may not have them next year.

Many companies use AI to at least give a first pass through the candidates, some even doing the first interview. We could do the same. AI would certainly do a more thorough job reading candidates' statements, papers and recommendation letters than we do, especially for those applying from universities we know less about. An AI interview could check how well a candidate understands their research and the role they played. But I suspect CS departments would feel queasy about offloading these processes.

A group of theory faculty, responding to a Simons Institute working group report, put out a statement about hiring for the AI age. You could do worse than following these guidelines.

  1. Emphasize quality over quantity. In the evaluations of candidates, consider at most three works from July 2026 onwards (of the candidates’ choosing), in addition to any number of prior works before July 2026.
  2. Actively assess thorough understanding. Evaluate the thoroughness of the candidates’ understanding of the aforementioned works more than was done normally until now. This evaluation could take the form of a “chalk talk,” more mathematically substantial interview slots, and/or other methods of the department’s choosing.

Why did it take the AI era for us to finally put quality over quantity?

entry.title: A More Impressive Use of AI than Proving the Unique Game Conjecture
entry.content:
I have a website devoted to parodies of the song

               I am the very model of a modern major general 

here. So I sometimes look around the web for more.  I recently came across

                                We are the very models of the throwback starfleet criminals

here. The tune isn't really the tune of I am...general but it's very impressive, especially to someone over 60 who both knows Star Trek and does not know what technology can do. 

a) It is NOT sung by fans in costume. (More on that later.)  It's actually sung by the actors who played those roles, in the costumes they wore for the show. What's really impressive is that all of the actors are dead.

b) The images looked just like the characters, and the voices sounded just like the characters.

c) I assume AI was involved. How much? Did AI write the song? Do I care so long as it's funny?

d) My main point: this would have been impossible X years ago for some value of X (readers--what do you think X is?) and hence I am impressed.  How old do you have to be to keep being impressed by these things?  And when will it stop being impressive?  Lance had a blog post about impressive visual effects in movies becoming standard and hence not impressive, see here.

e) It was really very good! Of course, as a fan of novelty songs, Gilbert and Sullivan, and Star Trek, I am predisposed to like it.

f) To understand the entire song you need to have watched three specific episodes recently.  This reminds me of a prior post see here about technology making it possible to produce good songs about niche topics. 

After seeing that video, I looked around for more Star Trek songs.  I found quite a few, here are my favorites:

------------------------------

A song about Dr. McCoy to the tune of The Devil went down to Georgia.The song's title is I'm a doctor not a ...  It's here

A song about Miles O'Brien (ST:DSN), to the tune of  I'm Gonna Be (500 miles).  The song's title is  I would fix 500 faults. It's here. I'm impressed with the video and with anyone who can identify every episode it refers to. 

A song about Picard trying to talk to a Tamarian, a species that only talks in metaphor, to the tune of Walk like an Egyptian. The song's title is Talk like a Tamarian. It's here.  It's based on one episode, Darmok. That's niche!

A song about the episode of Shore Leave from ST-TOS, to the tune of Life in Wartime.  The song's title is Life During Shore Team. It's here



----------------------------------
So, AI is producing really good star trek music videos with the actors from the show singing and playing instruments (I know it's not really them but it the images are just like them.) Is there a downside? For me, as a fan, this is great. 

But there are also YouTube videos made by fans (I presume they are fans) playing the roles. So they don't look like the characters, the songs aren't as clever as the AI-generated material (there are probably exceptions). I am sure it's still FUN for them. But will they stop doing it and have AI do it for them? If so then have we, as a culture, lost something?  More generally, if writers depend too much on AI we may lose the ability as a society to produce original material. And past some point AI might run out of material to use.

Here are some fan-produced music videos:

Lets Get Logical

Oh what a fight

Hit it Warp Five This one is based on ST-SNW. Contrast: ST-TOS was on TV in the 1960's when there were a very limited number of channels. ST-SNW is on Paramount+ which you either need to pay for or watch at your mom's house and your nephew's house (that's what I do) so there just aren't that many people watching. Hence this song may win the award for most niche. And niche wins the award for word-of-the-day.

entry.title: Fall Jobs Post 2026
entry.content:
Each fall I try to predict the upcoming job market for theoretical computer science faculty and give suggestions to those pursuing these positions. Last year I wrote that we should get set for a rocky ride, with AI’s disruption of computer science, fiscal stress at universities, and new U.S. policies affecting visas and funding.

Rocky indeed. The job market for computer science graduates continues to decline and with it undergraduate enrollment in the discipline. That should crater demand for CS professors, but anecdotally I'm seeing quite a few departments advertising multiple slots. Perhaps as more computer science departments create Artificial Intelligence programs, deans see the need for continued growth in computing.

Mostly though we're seeing hiring at schools with reasonably good finances, those with large endowments and state flagship universities. Many other schools are struggling and having hiring cutbacks or outright freezes. So I expect the strongest theory students will still find good positions but the second tier might be more challenging than in the past. Oddly enough, a candidate may have an easier time landing a job at a top university than at a mid-tier one.

I'm pessimistic that the recent elections will change much, at least for the next couple of years. Democrats won't make higher education a priority issue. At best they will slow the development of AI but it will continue to disrupt not just computer science but all of higher ed. Trump will remain president for two more years so I don't expect we'll see major changes in visa policy, at least not in a positive direction. Other causes of financial stress, including Baumol's cost disease, the tough job market for new computer science graduates, the public perception of higher education, and the demographic cliff will not go away. Perhaps universities will learn how to use artificial intelligence to cut costs but I'm not holding my breath.

On the positive side, Congress could use the appropriations process to reopen the NSF spigot, though that could take years to play out.

On to specific advice for students on the academic job market. 

CATCS maintains a Theoretical Computer Science Jobs posting site. More generally in computer science, there is the CRA Database of Job Candidates and the CRA and ACM job postings. 

Don't shy away from artificial intelligence. Make sure you talk about AI in both your research and teaching statements. Departments will need instructors who can teach the courses in all the new AI majors popping up.

Have a well-designed website with all your job materials and links to your papers (AI can help). Make sure your Google Scholar, LinkedIn and GitHub (if relevant) sites are accurate and up to date. Make a short video describing your research to a general computer science crowd. Take advantage of all the links above. Reach out directly to professors you know at schools you are interested in. And start now.

entry.title: Demaine-Gasarch-Hajiaghayi have written a book that is a sequel to Garey and Johnson
entry.content:
LANCE: You should take a break from all the AI stuff and talk about your book!

BILL: I will!  But it's not my book its co-authored with Erik Demaine and Mohammad Hajiaghayi. The title is

Computational Intractability: A Guide to Algorithmic Lower Bounds

LANCE: That sounds similar to Garey and Johnson's classic

Computers and Intractability: A Guide to the Theory of NP-Completeness

BILL: Indeed. DGH is a sequel to Garey and Johnson.

LANCE: But so much has happened since 1979.

BILL: Yes. That's why the book is over 500 pages and still does not cover everything since 1979.

LANCE: So what IS in the book?

BILL: The main question that drives complexity theory (and many other fields) is the question:

                Given a problem, how hard is it?

LANCE: Oh, You mean like P and NP!

BILL: Yes, but there is more! We cover P and NP: Many problems are proven NP-complete. Some are on Puzzles and Games. 

Examples of NP-Complete Problems that you might not have heard of

Disk Packing: Given a set of disks and a target square, can you place the disks so that they do not overlap and all of their centers lie within the square? This is Strongly NP-hard. 

Mate-in-1: Given a position in Settlers of Catan, can the player who is about to go win? This is NP-complete

Losing Checkers: Given a position in Checkers, is there a move that forces your opponent to win? This is  NP-complete. This is an important problem in case you play Checkers with a  Wookie, see here.

Super Mario Brothers and Many other Nintendo Games: Given a position in the game, and a level, can the player get to that level? This is NP-complete. (There are versions that are PSPACE-complete and versions that are undecidable)

Some use the machinery developed since G & J to show lower bounds on approximation:

VC with vertices of degree \(\le 3\): If there is a polytime \((\frac{145}{144}-\epsilon)\)-approx then P=NP.

We have a chapter on the Unique Games Conj--uh, uh, Theorem. 

We look BELOW NP: 3SUM-hardness, APSP-hardness (these are both a bit outdated), streaming algorithms, online algorithms, others.

We look ABOVE NP: #P, ETR,  

LANCE: What's ETR?

BILL: Existential Theory of the Reals is the following problem: Given a sentence of the form 

\((\exists x_1)(\exists x_2)\cdots(\exists x_n)[ C_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge C_k]\)

where each \(C_i\) is a polynomial equality or inequality in \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\)

is this sentence, with the quantifiers going over the reals, true?

Tarski proved ETR is decidable. ETR is known to be NP-hard and is thought to be harder than NP. 

A problem is ETR-complete if it is equivalent to ETR. This is a way to classify some problems that involve reals that were hard to classify with more traditional classes. For example, the Art Gallery Problem (how many guards do you need) is ETR-complete

LANCE: What else do you have that's above NP? 

BILL:  Poly Hierarchy, PSPACE, and even undecidability.

LANCE: Are there really NEW results about undecidability?

BILL: There are some video games where questions about winning are undecidable. I doubt Turing knew that. One of them is called braid (see here).

LANCE: Don't you have whole chapters devoted to the now-defunct Exponential Time Hypothesis and the 3-SUM conjecture?

Bill: Also the APSP conjecture. Are these now-defunct conjectures still worth studying? I did a blog post on that here. Do you read my blog posts?

LANCE: Do you read mine?

BILL: Fair point.

LANCE: Despite having three chapters obsolete, the rest of the book sounds great. Where can I get it?

BILL: You can buy it on Amazon, see here. You can buy it at MIT press here. You can download a prior draft here.

entry.title: Another Step Towards Optiland
entry.content:
When the Clay Mathematics Institute announced the Millennium Prize Problems back in 2000, we joked that if you proved P = NP, you wouldn't only get the $1 million prize for solving P v NP, but you would get $7 million since you could use P = NP to solve the rest.

In theory, if P = NP, then you could efficiently find the proof of any theorem, provided its formal proof was not too long. In practice, we don't have P = NP, and back then we didn't even have a good way to formalize a proof. Fast forward to today and we have a computer generated formalized proof of Navier-Stokes and a number of other important problems.

In my 2022 CACM article, I argued that we were heading towards Optiland, where we got all of the goodies of P = NP, without losing cryptography. But some challenges remained.
Machine learning seems to fail learning simple arithmetic—for example, summing up a large collection of numbers or multiplying large numbers. One could imagine combining machine learning with symbolic mathematical tools. While we’ve seen some impressive advances in theorem provers, we sit a long way from my dream task of taking one of my research papers, with its informal proofs, and having an AI system fill in the details and verify the proof.

I failed to imagine that in less than five years AI models would not just fill in the details of my proofs but find the proofs themselves.

Still plenty of math problems that AI hasn't solved, including P v NP itself. I've given up predicting what AI will prove next, though I still believe P v NP requires new techniques that AI won't come up with on its own.

I watch discussions on whether we could find some version of the ETH-refutation algorithm that would help solve SAT problems in practice. Spoiler alert: It will never beat CDCL.

We are running out of examples of real-world problems we still need P = NP to tackle. Outside of breaking codes, what could you do with P = NP that you couldn't do today using other means?

entry.title: 3SUM and APSP and ETH, Oh My!
entry.content:
(Throughout this post I will assume that the recent results by OpenAI and Anthropic contain correct proofs of what they claim.)

I wrote the following about 2 years ago but did not post it. It's dated, but that's the point.

BEGIN DOCUMENT FROM TWO YEARS AGO

Why do we think \(P\ne NP\)?

a) Lots of people have worked on SAT and other NP-complete problems, without getting them in P.  This is not mathematical evidence but it is worth noting.

b) If SAT is in P then all problems in NP are in P.  This implication is one reason I think \(P\ne NP\) is true.  I find this more compelling than (a), though it's still not a proof.

c) Just my opinion: I think SAT is not in P.

-------------------------

3SUM is the following problem: Given integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) is there a triple of indices \(i< j < k \) such that \(a_i + a_j + a_k = 0\)?  There is a clever algorithm for this problem that takes \(O(n^2)\) time. It is conjectured that 3SUM has no subquadratic algorithm (that is, for every fixed \(\epsilon>0\) there is no \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\) algorithm). (My spellcheck doesn't think subquadratic is a word. Are they right?) 

This conjecture is widely believed. There is a notion of 3SUM-hardness and 3SUM-completeness.  \( A \le B \) if there is a linear time function \(f\) such that \(x\in A\)  iff \(f(x)\in B\).  A problem \(A\) is 3SUM-complete if both \(A\le 3SUM\) and \(3SUM \le A\).

There are around 15-20 3SUM-complete problems.  Either they are all subquadratic (which includes 3SUM being subquadratic) or none are subquadratic.  Given the conjecture, none of them are subquadratic.  That is the common belief.

Why do we think 3SUM has no subquadratic algorithm?

a) Lots of people have worked on 3SUM without getting it into subquadratic time.  This is not mathematical evidence but it is worth noting.

b) Darn! There is no Cook-Levin-type theorem for 3SUM.

c) Just my opinion: I think 3SUM is not subquadratic. I only wish there were a Cook-Levin-type theorem for this belief. I doubt this is possible.

--------------------------

APSP (All Pairs Shortest Paths) is the following problem: Given a weighted graph \(G\), find, for all pairs, the cost of the shortest path.  There is an \(O(n^3\)) algorithm for APSP. It is widely believed that there is no subcubic algorithm for APSP (that is, for every fixed \(\epsilon>0\) there is no \(O(n^{3-\epsilon})\) algorithm).  This conjecture is widely believed. There is a notion of APSP-hardness and APSP-completeness.  \( A \le B \) if there is a linear time function \(f\) such that \(x\in A\) iff  \(f(x) \in B\).  A problem \(A\) is APSP-complete if both \(A\le APSP\) and \(APSP \le A\). (My spellcheck doesn't think subcubic is a word. Are they right?)

There are around 15-20 problems that are APSP-complete.  Either they are all subcubic (which includes APSP being subcubic) or none are subcubic.  Given the conjecture, none of them are subcubic.  That is the common belief.

Why do we think APSP has no subcubic algorithm?

(a) and (b) similar to that for 3SUM. I state (c)

c) Just my opinion: I think APSP is not subcubic. I only wish there were a Cook-Levin-type theorem for this belief. I doubt this is possible.

---------------------------

ETH (Exponential Time Hypothesis) Not only is 3SAT not in P but 3SAT on \(n\) variables requires \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) time.  ETH is widely believed.

Informally, if ETH is true, and \(A\) is NP-complete by a linear reduction, then \(A\) requires exponential time. There are many such NP-complete problems.

(a) and (b) similar to that for 3SUM. I state (c)

c) Just my opinion: I think 3SAT requires \(2^{cn}\) time for some \(c\).  I only wish there was a Cook-Levin-type theorem for this belief. I doubt this is possible.

END DOCUMENT FROM TWO YEARS AGO

Three of my favorite hardness assumptions had a bad month. I'm glad the Unique Game Conjecture was proven true so I am 1-for-4 rather than 0-for-3 (if it were still open) or 0-for-4 (if it was refuted).

1) Anthropic has obtained an \(O(n^{1.9992})\) algorithm for 3SUM.  Darling thinks this result is hilarious.

A writeup of this by J. Alman and V.V. Williams is here.  

2) Anthropic has obtained an \(O(n^{2.9995})\) algorithm for APSP with integer weights (with no negative cycles).  Darling, thinks this result is hilarious. (Spell check thinks Antrhopic is a word. Are they right?) 

The same writeup in item (1) also contains this result.

3) OpenAI has obtained a \(2^{O(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}\) algorithm for 3SAT Darling thinks this result is hilarious. I agree with her. (My spellcheck things OpenAI is not a word. Are they right?)

OpenAI's announcement is here.

Lance blogged about it here.

So now what?

0) All of these results are being looked at by experts.

1) 1.9992 is close to 2. And we still think 3SUM can't get that much better. could conjecture that, for every fixed \(\epsilon\), there is no \(O(n^{1.5-\epsilon})\) algorithm for \(3SUM\).

Assuming the conjecture, for every fixed \(\epsilon\), for every 3SUM-complete problem \(A\) there  is no  \(O(n^{1.5-\epsilon})\) algorithm for \(A\).

At least until AI gives an \(O(n^{1.499999})\) algorithm for 3SUM.

2) Similar for APSP and, say, \(O(n^{2.5})\).

3) ETH. Replace with the following: there exists \(0<c<1\) such that there is no \(O(2^{n^c})\) algorithm for \(3SAT\). Or something else like it.

4) We can Regard this as good news. All of those problems that are 3SUM-complete are now known to have subquadratic complexity. Similar for APSP and ETH. Yeah(?)

entry.title: The Exponential Time Refutation
entry.content:
In this week's big news (though it's only Wednesday), OpenAI announced a proof that the exponential-time hypothesis is false, with a Lean proof. Later Anthropic released their own paper. Ryan O'Donnell and Shiva Kintali posted follow-up proofs, smartly focusing on simplicity rather than getting the best bounds. OpenAI will partner with three of my favorite complexity theorists, Russell Impagliazzo, Mohan Paturi and Ryan Williams to verify and study the proof. I have not verified the proof myself, but it is safe to assume now that the exponential-time hypothesis is toast. 

Update (10/29): Impagliazzo, Paturi and Williams set up a site to discuss the ETH Refutation with a discussion blog and paper repository.

Recall 3-SAT, the problem of determining whether a Boolean formula that is an AND of ORs of three variables or their negations has a satisfying assignment. 3-SAT is the prototypical NP-complete problem from which we derive all the others. The exponential-time hypothesis (ETH), introduced by Impagliazzo and Paturi in 1999, building on their work with Francis Zane, states that there is a \(c > 0\) such that every algorithm solving 3-SAT requires time \(2^{cn}\), where \(n\) is the number of variables. There's also a strong exponential-time hypothesis (SETH) which says that for every \(\epsilon > 0\) there is a \(k\) such that \(k\)-SAT cannot be solved in time \(2^{(1-\epsilon)n}\). The OpenAI paper gives an algorithm that, for every fixed \(k\), determines whether a \(k\)-CNF formula with \(n\) variables and \(m\) clauses is satisfiable, and even counts the number of solutions, in time \((n+m)^{O(1)}\,2^{O(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}\) (their Lean proof gives a slightly weaker bound). This refutes ETH, and hence SETH, which implies ETH.

If you want to understand the proof, I suggest starting with Ryan O'Donnell's paper. Ryan also mentions Bernardo Subercaseaux's observation that we get a nontrivial simulation of nondeterministic time on multitape Turing machines, 
\[\mathrm{NTIME}(T) \subseteq \mathrm{DTIME}\left(2^{O(T(\log\log T)^3/\sqrt{\log T})}\right).\]
Researchers studied ETH and SETH because they implied many other hardness results, for example
  • If ETH is true then Clique requires time \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) on \(n\)-vertex graphs, or \(2^{\Omega(\sqrt{m})}\) on graphs with \(m\) edges.
  • If ETH is true then finding a clique of size \(k\) cannot be done in time \(f(k)\,n^{o(k)}\) for any computable function \(f\), so the trivial \(n^{O(k)}\) algorithm is essentially optimal.
  • If SETH is true then the orthogonal vectors problem on \(n\) vectors of dimension \(\omega(\log n)\) cannot be solved in time \(n^{2-\epsilon}\) for any \(\epsilon > 0\).
Bill's new (badly timed) book with Erik Demaine and Mohammad Hajiaghayi has details. The fact that ETH and SETH fail doesn't mean their implications are false.

Keep in mind that the OpenAI algorithm applies to \(k\)-SAT but not to NP problems in general. It gives nothing new for Subset Sum or Traveling Salesman, whose best algorithms still take roughly \(2^{n/2}\) and \(2^n\) time, because the reductions from those problems to 3-SAT blow up the number of variables too much. Getting subexponential algorithms for all of NP would require solving 3-SAT in time \(2^{n^{o(1)}}\mathrm{,}\) which the OpenAI result doesn't get close to achieving.

entry.title: When is it plausible that a result is optimal?
entry.content:
(Lance and Bill did a vidcast about the OpenAI Document Drop. See here. My spellcheck thinks that vidcast and OpenAI are not words.) 


 The Metric TSP problem is TSP where, for all vertices \(x,y,z\), 

                                    \(w(x,z) \le  w(x,y) + w(y,z) \).

In 1976 Christofides and Serdyukov (independently of each other) showed that there is a poly time algorithm for a 1.5-approx to Metric TSP.

Some people thought the 1.5 could be improved.

Some people thought that 1.5 is optimal. 

1.5 is a natural number. Hmm, that's not quite right. 1.5 is a  pretty number. It would not be a surprise if someone had proven 

                                   If there is a poly time (\(1.5-\epsilon\)) approx then P=NP.

Indeed, people tried to prove that. 

In 2020 Anna R. Karlin, Nathan Klein, and Shayan Oveis  Gharan  proved 

                                  there is a poly time (\(1.5-\frac{1}{10^{36}}\))  approximation algorithm. 

Darling thinks this result is hilarious. I tried to tell her that the result is important since 

a) We now know that 1.5 is NOT optimal.

b) One of the authors, Nathan Klein, had been in my REU program in 2015.

c) The arxiv version has one author using their middle initial, one author doing nothing for their middle name, and one author spelling out their entire middle name. I think that's unusual. 

She was not impressed.

Nobody believes that \(1.5-\frac{1}{10^{36}}\) is optimal. 

Is there a current conjecture? Klein told me he thinks  4/3.  A pretty number. 

The recent results on Matrix Mult and  Int Mult give a contrast involving pretty runtime and ugly runtimes.

MATRIX MULT

Let \(\omega\) be the least \(a\) such that two \(n\times n\) matrices can be multiplied together with \(O(n^a)\) operations. This definition is not quite right for two reasons:

(i) It is possible (though I think unlikely) that there is no least \(a\), For example, if there is a sequence of algorithms with runtime \(O(n^{2.1})\), \(O(n^{2.01})\), \(O(n^{2.001})\), \(\ldots\), then there is no least \(a\),

(ii) It is possible (though I thought unlikely before Oct 6, 2026), that the runtime may be different over different fields. 

We keep the incorrect definition to prove that ChatGPT is not the boss of me.

Here are some known results. I may have missed some:

The traditional algorithm: \(\omega\le 3\).

Strassen's Algorithm (1969): \(\omega\le \log_2 7 = 2.807\ldots \).

Coppersmith-Winograd (1990): \(\omega \le 2.376\ldots \).

Stothers (2010): \(\omega \le 2.3736\ldots\).

V.V. Williams (2012): \(\omega \le 2.3728642\ldots \).  (Stothers and V.V. Williams were independent.)

Alman and V.V. Williams (2020): \(\omega < 2.3728596\).

Alman, Duan, V.V. Williams, Y. Xu, Z. Xu, and Zhou (2024):  \(\omega < 2.371339 \).  (The preprint was in 2024. The published paper was in 2025.)

Google DeepMind's AI-based optimizer (August 2026): \(\omega < 2.371177\).

The value 2.371177 was the best upper bound on \(\omega\) for about 2 months.

The Chrysler Building was the tallest building in the world for about 11 months: from May 27, 1930 until May 1, 1931. The Empire State Building was the new champion. After May 1, 1931, the Chrysler Building wasn't even the tallest building in Manhattan. Fame is fleeting in both mathematics and architecture.

Note:

a) I believe that all of the algorithms above work over any field.

Google AI agrees with that, but ChatGPT correctly reminded me that Google AI's opinion is not a proof and that I should seek a citation or a counterexample.  If you know of a citation to confirm the any-field statement, or a counterexample to the any-field statement, please leave a comment.

b) After 1990 the improvements are really small.

c) None of these bounds is a pretty candidate for the true exponent.

We need notation that makes the field explicit.

Let \(\mathbb{F}\) be a field.  Let \(\omega(\mathbb{F})\) be the least \(a\) such that two \(n\times n\) matrices over \(\mathbb{F}\) can be multiplied together with \(O(n^a)\) operations.  (ChatGPT is still not the boss of me.)

OpenAI showed the following:

a) \(\omega(\mathbb{C})\le 2.25\). 2.25 is a very pretty number. It makes my heart go pitter-patter.

b) For every field \(\mathbb{F}\) they have \(\omega(\mathbb{F}) < 2.371054886006746\).

Lean-formalized.

A separate GitHub project claims to extend the 2.25 bound to every field with a Lean-checked proof. I have not checked the extension (as opposed to all of the new results OpenAI has dropped, which I have checked line by line with a quill pen and inkwell by the light of an oil lamp). The project is here.


Back to the issue at hand.

The drop from \(\omega \le 2.37\) to \(2.25\) is a Bob Beamon moment. Recall that before the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City, the world record for the long jump was 27 feet, 4.75 inches (8.35 meters). During those Olympics, Bob Beamon jumped 29 feet, 2.5 inches (8.9 meters). A massive improvement. His record stood until 1991, when Mike Powell jumped 29 feet, 4.5 inches (8.95 meters). Gee, only two inches more! Mike Powell's jump still holds the record. So Beamon had the record for 23 years, and Powell has the record for 35 years.  If matrix multiplication follows the same pattern, we may wait 23 years for the next improvement and 35 more years for the one after that. However, since we are dealing with silicon instead of carbon, it may be 23 days and 35 days.

I am happy that the new upper bound on \(\omega\) is a pretty number and hence a plausible candidate for optimal.  If no one improves the result within 23 days, I will think 2.25 is optimal.

INT MULT

 Improved Algorithms for Integer Multiplication of two \(n\)-bit numbers.

In 1971 Schonhage and Strassen conjectured that there is an algorithm for integer multiplication that takes \(O(n\log n)\) bit operations.  In 2019, Harvey and van der Hoeven proved this conjecture.  Is there an algorithm that takes less time? Or is \(O(n\log n)\) optimal?

OpenAI obtained an algorithm that takes \(O(n(\log n)^{1-\kappa})\) bit operations, where \(\kappa=2^{-82}\). Really? \(2^{-82}\)? I declined to tell Darling about this one.

Google tells me that OpenAI did not lean-verify this one but open-source contributors later completed an independent Lean verification of the algorithm and improved the bound. The link is here. The improvement first pushed the small term to \(2^{-34}\) and then to \(2^{-14.38}\). I won't tell Darling these results until its down to \(2^{-1}\). 

Note the contrast between matrix multiplication and integer multiplication.

Matrix multiplication went from a runtime too ugly to be optimal---(O(n^{2.371\ldots})\)---to one pretty enough to be optimal---\(O(n^{2.25})\).  

Integer multiplication went from a runtime pretty enough to be optimal---\(O(n\log n)\)---to one too ugly to be optimal---\(O(n(\log n)^{1-\kappa})\), where \(\kappa=2^{-14.38}\)

entry.title: Reading Messy Proofs
entry.content:
In fall of 1985 when I started graduate school, my advisor Michael Sipser asked me to read an early handwritten manuscript by Johan Håstad of his switching lemma. I spent many hours decoding the notation and working through the messy conditional probabilities until I felt I had checked every step of the proof. When I started presenting this to Sipser, he stopped me and said he didn't want the details but instead the intuition of the proof. I had nothing.

I'm reminded of this story as I hear the complaints of how badly OpenAI wrote the 712 papers released on October 6th, as though humans wrote crystal-clear proofs beforehand, definitely not the case in general, especially in the early versions.

Noam Nisan once told me that reading a badly written proof leads to better understanding since you really need to figure out the details instead of having them neatly spelled out. Perhaps, but do not use this as an excuse for not taking the time to write the details properly.

I approach reading the proof of a new result by assuming the proof is wrong until I'm convinced otherwise. Working my way through early versions of Immerman-Szelepcsényi and Toda's theorem definitely forced me to understand these proofs well so I could explain them to others.

I just gave up on fully understanding some results like the original PCP theorem and Ran Raz's Parallel Repetition Theorem, despite seeing the authors give talks on the papers. Sometimes you have to trust the authors and others who hopefully have read the paper. Don't even get me started on László Babai's Graph Isomorphism in quasipolynomial time. And some papers, like Primes in P, require mathematical results in other subfields that I just have to accept.

Sometimes you'll just get better versions of proofs, most famously Irit Dinur's combinatorial proof of the PCP theorem. I only really understood the switching lemma years later when Sophie Laplante and I wrote a Kolmogorov complexity-based proof building on a then-new proof of Alexander Razborov.

When I get stuck in a proof, I sometimes ask the authors, but usually as a last resort unless I can talk to them in person. That's an advantage we have now: you can ask AI to get you over a hurdle in a proof. Claude, while maybe not as good at proving theorems as the unreleased OpenAI model, does a better job writing them up. And one hopes that we'll see simplified and possibly strengthened versions of some of these important results, written by humans or human-AI collaborations. Maybe we'll even get the intuition Sipser told me to seek all those years ago.

entry.title: AI, Math, the document-drop. Non-Tech Thoughts
entry.content:
So what to make of OpenAI and the future of Math? Here are some points I've either:

thought of myself or heard from a human or read from an AI.

Throughout this post I use the term AI to mean an AI system that produces mathematical results.  I decline to say  OpenAI or  Anthropic as generic terms since about 20 years ago I used  Intrade  as a generic term for Betting Markets---then Intrade went out of business.  I wish I had bet on that happening. Oh well.

1) Some of the proofs were Lean-formalized and some were not.  If a proof is Lean-verified do we know the proof is valid?  The issue is not bugs in Lean.  The issue is that coding a theorem/proof into Lean may be done incorrectly. So Lean might be verifying a proof of a theorem different than what was intended.

Peter Woit, is a string-theory skeptic and a Lean-skeptic. See here

Alexander Bastounis, Fabian Circelli, Anders Hansen argue that the Lean formalization does not correspond to the natural-language proof. See here  

My impression/predictions are:

(1) Lean has a good track record BUT we are in uncharted territory here.

(2) In the end humans will read, understand, and fix the proofs if necessary. This will take time. 

(3) Humans will produce readable writeups that are enlightening. This will take time. 

(4) Some bugs in Lean will be discovered and fixed. This will take time.

(5) Humans will learn how to better code theorems and proofs into the Lean language. This will take time.

2) Most (all?) of the papers were hard to read, even by experts.  Lance asked Claude for a better written version of UGC and he got one: here.  Why didn't OpenAI ask Claude for better writeups?

3) A History of my thought on the Unique Game Conjecture:

In 2006 I thought the Unique Game Conjecture would be proved by 2011. I was wrong.

In 2016 I thought the Unique Game Conjecture would be proved by 2026.  I was right.

In 2026 I thought the Unique Game Conjecture would be proved by 2046. I was right literally but wrong really since in January 2026 I was thinking 10-20 years, not 7 months.

4) Right now AI is merely combining known ideas and writing up the proofs badly as opposed to most mathematicians who come up with new ideas and they write them up well. I am, of course, kidding.

5) There have been barrier results along the lines of  Technique X will not suffice to prove Y' Some papers say this informally, e.g.,  our methods cannot be extended and some papers say this formally, e.g.,  since there are oracles that force P=NP and oracles that force \(P\ne NP\), relativizing techniques do not suffice to resolve P versus NP  (My PhD is on oracles, yet I replaced  recursion-theoretic techniques with  relativizing techniques because ChatGPT is the boss of me.)

What we really want to prove is that known techniques won't solve a problem, hence we need to look for new techniques.

If problem X has not been solved within 10 years by AI, then is it safe to assume that known techniques will not suffice?

Probably not:

a) AI will not make all connections between all the parts of math within 10 years, maybe not ever.

b) AI companies might stop having their machines work on math problems. I'm surprised they are doing that now since mathematicians who want to solve open problems are not a big market. Then again, they could advertise as follows: Buy Our Theorem Prover and you Might Solve a $1,000,000 Math Problem!!! or a Salmon (see here)!!!

6) The notion that AI is combining known ideas is true but is not a problem. However, might the following happen: What if within 10 years all math that can be done with known techniques will have been done.  Then either

a) Humans will step up to the plate and come up with new ideas.  Let's hope they never stopped.

b) Humans will have lost the ability to come up with new ideas because they will have been spoiled by AI.  Like if Lance and I had to become hunter-gatherer. Lance's initials would then stand for Lion Food, and Bill's  initials would stand for Bear Grub. (I came up with Lion Food, but I asked Gemini for Bear Grub. I doubt you care. AI-disclosure can be stupid.)

c) AI will be able to come up with new ideas. The current LLM models probably can't do that but they may help design something that can.

d) As noted in comments 5, AI companies might give up on this line of work.

7) When Deep Blue beat Kasparov an ordinary citizen could not purchase a computer that would play grandmaster-level chess. Now an ordinary citizen can download for free a chess playing program that can beat the world chess champion.

Will this happen with AI for Math?  Will an ordinary citizen be able to download for free, or pay a reasonable price for, an AI program that can prove hard theorems?

8) AI-assisted vs AI-generated may be a big distinction. Or not. Or it may be hard to tell the difference.

I can imagine working on a project where I do some, an AI does some, and I don't really want to figure out and report on who did what part. Similar to human co-authors today. This comes up when one of my HS students enters the Regeneron Science Talent Search and the forms ask in 16 different ways What was their contribution  and  What was your contribution? In the future will they ask  What was the AI contribution? 

9) Hypothetical:

I ask  AI to prove \(P\ne NP\) and it gives me a proof that I rewrite to be readable.  I submit it to STOC, honestly acknowledging what my contribution was, which is mostly exposition.  Assume I meet the ACM authorship criteria.

a) Is the fact that I used AI held against me?

b) Should the paper get in?

c) Do I get the Millennium Prize and hence $1,000,000?

d) Do I win a Turing Award and hence another $1,000,000?

10) How is OpenAI making money on this? Three sources that I know of, New Scientist, Science Magazine, and Crypto Briefing (I am having trouble getting the links to work) put the cost at around 15 million dollars.  After OpenAI spent that much money solving a Millennium problem, they stated that they would not try to collect the $1,000,000 (it's not clear they would have qualified for it). That seems odd.  What is their business model? To generate buzz? If so then note the following:

I have asked my non-math friends (Lance is surprised I have non-math friends) if they have heard about the OpenAI Document Drop.  No. Some had vaguely heard that AI solved an important problem that was worth some money, I assume that's Navier-Stokes, but that's it. No buzz.

The Atlantic Monthly has published an article about this titled OpenAI Just Carpet-Bombed Mathematics (see here)   This will give OpenAI more publicity.  Is it good or bad publicity?  There is a famous quote there is no such thing as bad publicity.  Is it true? See here.

As I finish this post (Translation: As I argue with Chatty about this post) OpenAI has announced that it will give $5 million to the Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.  That may help explain its community engagement, but the existence of a business model is still an open question.

As I finish this post (Translation: As I argue with my AI-skeptical proofreader) my proofreader announced that he knows OpenAI's business model:

Delusion and IPO or Delusion plus PR to get more funding. The IPO is looking less likely.

Is he right? Is that really a business model?  

Here is a link about the business model: here.


I wrote most of this blog post  on Tuesday Oct 13, 2026. I posted it on Oct 18, 2026. Between Oct 13 and Oct 18 the post aged: at a funeral I went to today (Oct 16, 2026-Boss's day!) non-math people asked me  Now that OpenAI can solve open math problems, how do you stop your students from cheating on homework? So non-math people have heard the news, though they don't quite understand it.

11)  I told my Mom that AI had solved some problems that I cared about and that I was happy about that. She asked  Can  AI  fix my answering machine and then have Lean verify that it works?

12) On  Scott's blog (see here), comment number 12 by Tristan, perhaps unintentionally, raised an interesting question. Here are some quotes from Tristan's comment:

But perhaps the occasion calls for a little reflection. If a pattern-interpolating autocomplete can produce your theorem quite so readily, one is entitled to wonder how intellectually demanding the enterprise was to begin with. Perhaps what you took for creativity and insight was, on closer inspection, neither.

Algebraic geometry [Tristan's field] is, mercifully, a field in which genuine creativity remains indispensable: one must actually conceive and construct new mathematical objects, rather than rearrange familiar patterns and dignify the exercise with the word `discovery'. It is precisely this sort of work that lies beyond the capacities of a glorified autocomplete.

a) Such elegant arrogance! Such elegant nonsense! Such arrogant nonsense!

b) This is the kind of quote that will age badly once OpenAI begins solving problems in Algebraic Geometry.

c) I disagree with him: there are easy and hard problems in all fields of math. Algebraic Geometry is an older field, so perhaps there is less low-hanging fruit. But this is a minor point and not the fundamental difference he makes it out to be. And I hardly call the Unique Game Conjecture or L=RL low hanging fruit.

d) Still, to turn his thoughts into  an intelligent question: What types of math problems are more prone to have AI solve them?

e) Scott later left the comment:

LOL! That was a delightful parody (at least, I assume it's a parody) of what I've now heard dozens of times in earnest.

Bill here: I FELL FOR IT.

f) Anon later left a comment that flagged Tristan's post as AI-generated by running it through an AI program to detect AI-generated writings: here.

Bill here: I NEVER SUSPECTED IT WAS AI. FROM NOW ON I WILL SUSPECT EVERYTHING IS AI.

13) A 1985 article in Kvant, a Soviet Mathematics Magazine, by Uspenskii and Semenov, titled Solvable and Unsolvable Algorithmic Problems, contained the following quote:

Tarski's result [that elementary geometry is decidable] appears to be, and actually is, extremely powerful and even paradoxical.  There is a very extensive area of classical mathematics (namely elementary geometry) which is traditionally thought to require a subtle intellect and which can by no means be reduced to carrying out routine computations, and yet, at the same time, there is an algorithm that can verify the truth of theorems in the area (and provide the proofs). We can console ourselves only in the fact that Tarski's algorithm is not realistic: it requires an inconceivably great amount of time for its implementation.

I leave it to the reader to adapt this quote to the current situation. Or not.

14) So what now for mathematicians? For Math grad students?

a) OpenAI says its model attempted roughly 4000 problems and reported results for 372 families, some full and some partial. So there is still plenty that OpenAI can't do.  But who knows what the future will bring?

b) There are plenty more problems that OpenAI was not given.

c) There is a lot more to research than research. (Both ChatGPT and my proofreader think the last sentence was a typo. It's not.) There are surveys, blogs, raising questions, and rewriting proofs so they are readable.  Will Tenure committees, the NSF,  and others,  see it that way?

e) I wonder if in the future the quality of exposition may be more important since the journals and conferences will just assume that the brilliant ideas were done by AI and give the human less credit. If Math dissertations end up being more readable, I call that a win.

entry.title: Complexity and Lean
entry.content:
In the OpenAI Math Drop some papers have Lean proofs, others don't, including L = RL = BPL. Why is it hard to formalize results on complexity classes?

Let's consider an example, Lautemann's proof that BPP is in \(\Sigma^p_2\). It's a beautiful proof because it comes down to a single formula. I gave the full proof in a 2025 post, but to remind you, here is the setup.

Let \(B\) be in BPP, accepted by a probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machine \(M\) with error bounded by \(2^{-n}\). Let \(A(x,r)\) be true iff \(M(x)\) using random tape \(r\) accepts. \(A(x,r)\) is deterministically polynomial-time computable. We can assume \(|r|=|x|^k\) for some \(k\).

Here is the \(\Sigma^p_2\) expression for input \(x\) of length \(n\). All quantification is over binary strings of length \(n^k\). Let \(\oplus\) be bitwise parity (XOR) and \(\vee\) be logical OR.

\[\exists z_1,\ldots,z_{n^k}\ \forall y\ \ A(x,z_1\oplus y) \vee \cdots \vee A(x,z_{n^k}\oplus y)\]

The hard part of the proof, besides coming up with this formula itself, is the probabilistic argument to show you always get the right answer.

So this seems simple enough to give a full Lean proof. And it is not too hard (for Claude) to get Lean to formalize the probabilistic argument, though even there Lean makes you deal with details we wave away on paper. When \(x\not\in B\) the argument needs \(n^k2^{-n}<1\), which fails for small \(n\), so short inputs need separate handling. But you also need to show the following:

Let \(A(x,r)\) be polynomial-time computable. Then given \(x\), \(y\) and the \(z_i\) as inputs, you can compute \(A(x,z_1\oplus y) \vee \cdots \vee A(x,z_{n^k}\oplus y)\) in polynomial time, where \(u\oplus v\) is bitwise parity.

There is nothing challenging about this statement. It is so painfully obviously true that I didn't even bring up this point in the 2025 post. But proving you can do this in polynomial time on a Turing machine, even though the only operations are bitwise parity, ORs and composition, is just very complicated to formalize in Lean.

Some suggest that using Cobham's characterization might be easier. But see below for what you need to do for bitwise parity alone. Imagine how complicated it would all get for something like Toda's theorem.

Update: Since I first drafted this post, OpenAI dropped a claimed Lean proof of L = RL = BPL, so maybe ignore this whole post?

Cobham defined his class as the smallest set of functions on the natural numbers (viewed as binary strings, with \(|x|\) the length of \(x\) and \(|0|=0\)) that contains the constant zero, the projections, the two successor functions \(s_0(x)=2x\) and \(s_1(x)=2x+1\), and the smash function \(x\#y=2^{|x|\cdot|y|}\), and that is closed under composition and bounded recursion on notation. The second operation defines a new function \(f\) from functions \(g\), \(h_0\), \(h_1\) in the class by \[\begin{aligned} f(0,\vec{y})&=g(\vec{y})\\ f(s_i(x),\vec{y})&=h_i(x,\vec{y},f(x,\vec{y})) \end{aligned}\] for \(i\in\{0,1\}\) and \(s_i(x)\neq 0\), provided that \(f(x,\vec{y})\leq k(x,\vec{y})\) for some \(k\) already in the class. The recursion runs over the bits of \(x\), so it takes only \(|x|\) steps. The smash function gives the outputs polynomial growth in their lengths, and the bound \(k\) keeps that growth from compounding over the recursion. Cobham's theorem says that this class is exactly the set of functions computable in polynomial time.

As an example, consider bitwise XOR, \(f(x,y)=x\oplus y\). The difficulty is that bounded recursion on notation peels bits off only one argument, while XOR has to move through \(x\) and \(y\) together. The fix is to recurse on a long enough counter \(T\) and extract the bits of \(x\) and \(y\) by shifting. We first need four helper functions, each defined by a single bounded recursion on notation: \[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{par}(0)=\mathrm{par}(s_0(x))&=0, & \mathrm{par}(s_1(x))&=1\\ \mathrm{half}(0)&=0, & \mathrm{half}(s_i(x))&=x\\ \mathrm{msp}(0,x)&=x, & \mathrm{msp}(s_i(w),x)&=\mathrm{half}(\mathrm{msp}(w,x))\\ C(0,u,v)=C(s_0(a),u,v)&=u, & C(s_1(a),u,v)&=v \end{aligned}\] with bounds \(1\), \(x\), \(x\) and \(s_1(u)\#s_1(v)\) respectively. Here \(\mathrm{msp}(w,x)=\lfloor x/2^{|w|}\rfloor\), so bit \(j\) of \(x\) is \(\mathrm{par}(\mathrm{msp}(w,x))\) for any \(w\) with \(|w|=j\). \(C\) is a conditional on the low bit of \(a\). Composition then gives the XOR of the low bits of \(a\) and \(c\), \(\beta(a,c)=C(a,\mathrm{par}(c),C(c,1,0))\), and appending the low bit of \(b\) to \(z\), \(\mathrm{app}(b,z)=C(b,s_0(z),s_1(z))\).

Now we recurse on \(w\) with \(T\), \(x\) and \(y\) as parameters, building the answer from the top bit down. Let \(m_i=\mathrm{msp}(s_i(w),T)\), which has length \(|T|-|w|-1\), the position of the next bit to append, and let \(b_i=\beta(\mathrm{msp}(m_i,x),\mathrm{msp}(m_i,y))\) be that bit of \(x\oplus y\). Then \[\begin{aligned} G(0,T,x,y)&=0\\ G(s_i(w),T,x,y)&=\mathrm{app}(b_i,G(w,T,x,y)) \end{aligned}\] By induction, \(G(w,T,x,y)\) is \(x\oplus y\) shifted right by \(|T|-|w|\) bits, so it is bounded by \(s_1(x)\#s_1(y)\). Finally we set \[f(x,y)=G(T,T,x,y)\quad\text{where } T=s_1(x)\#s_1(y).\] The smash gives \(|T|=(|x|+1)(|y|+1)+1\geq\max(|x|,|y|)\), so the recursion starts above the high bits of both arguments, where every bit is zero. \(T\) is much longer than it needs to be, but that costs only polynomially many extra steps.

entry.title: Conjectures that I thought would not be proved in my lifetime....were
entry.content:
Lance blogged on the OpenAI solutions to many problems here and also created a website of the TCS-related problems OpenAI claims to have solved here.

Terry Tao seems to have had an infinite number of guest bloggers talking about AI and Math even before the OpenAI .... WE NEED A WORD FOR IT. My proofreader suggests GARBARGE DUMP. I prefer the more neutral DOCUMENT DUMP. 

Scott blogged about what he calls the Mathocalypse

Peter Woit weighted in on what he calls the Slopocalypse.  He has many astute observations. Among them:  he has good reasons to think that Lean-formalized does not necessarily mean  that a proof is correct. For another skeptical-of-Lean viewpoint see here.

Now it's my turn to comment on the DOCUMENT DUMP. For now I will just discuss some of the results without getting into what it means for the future of mathematics, the future of academia, and the future of humanity.

--------------------------------

1)  Let \(G\) be the graph whose vertex set is \(\mathbb{R}^2\), with an edge between every pair of points exactly a unit distance apart.  The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is called the chromatic number of the plane. For nearly 70 years, all that was known was \( 4\le \chi\le 7\). We denote \(\chi(G)\) by \(\chi\).

The proof that \(4 \le\chi\) is easy.

The proof that \(\chi\le 7\) is easy.

In 2018, Aubrey de Grey improved the lower bound to 5.

The proof that \(5\le \chi\)  is hard: it involves a 1,581-vertex graph, later reduced to 509 vertices by Jaan Parts, who probably did it in parts.

The new result by OpenAI: \( 6\le \chi\).  Lean-formalized.

When I first heard that OpenAI had improved the lower bound I thought they did a clever search for a larger graph.

I was wrong.

OpenAI's proof took an entirely different approach. They proved the following:

a) If there is a proper 5-coloring of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), then there is a weak measurable proper 5-coloring.

b) There is no weak measurable proper 5-coloring of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).  Therefore, there is no proper 5-coloring of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

Was the idea of using measurable colorings new? No.

Measurable colorings had been studied before. Falconer showed that any measurable proper coloring of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) requires at least five colors.  This result rules out a measurable proper 4-coloring but allows the possibility of a measurable proper 5-coloring.  OpenAI's result rules out a proper 5-coloring even without a measurability assumption.  OpenAI used the notion of weak measurable colorings to obtain a result about all colorings. That is new.

This is a clear case of  Searching has reached its limits; we need a new approach  and OpenAI found one.

-----------------------------------------
2) The Erdős-Turán Conjecture. Let \(A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots \}\) be a set of positive integers such that \(\sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_i}\) diverges. Then \(A\) has arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

What was known? In 2020, Bloom and Sisask showed that \(A\) contains a 3-term arithmetic progression. See here.

The general result for 4-term progressions was open.

OpenAI proved the entire conjecture.  Lean-formalized.

This is widely considered a very hard problem. I didn't think this conjecture would be proven soon.  But it has been proven and Lean-formalized. I hope it soon becomes people-understood.

The  3-term case was hard. I thought that

(a) people might go on to prove the  4-term case, but

(b) anything beyond that was out of reach.

So I am very surprised to see a proof of the \(k\)-term case for all \(k\).

In my view, this is the most important and impressive of the new results.  Why? Of the results discussed, this one seemed least likely to be proven by humans and most likely to depend on deep mathematics. Did the proof by OpenAI use deep math? It looks that way to me.

------------------------------
3) Let W(k,r) be the least W such that, for every \(r\)-coloring of \(\{1,\ldots,W\}\), there is a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length \(k\). 

The best known upper bound:

                            \(W(k, r) \le 2^{2^{r^{2^{2^{k+9}}}}}\).

The best lower bound (before Document Drop Day):

                            \(W(k,r)\ge \beta r^{k-1}\) for some absolute constant \(\beta\).

The improvement: there is an absolute constant \(c\) such that, for every \(r\ge 2\) and sufficiently large \(k\), \(W(k,r)> k^{ck\lfloor \log_2 r\rfloor}\).  Lean-formalized.

I am not surprised at the result. I am surprised that the result has been proved.  For a long time, the best lower bound was roughly \(r^{k-1}\).  

Is this a big improvement? We think of \(r\) as small and \(k\) as big so yes.

The paper that OpenAI put out on this misquotes the prior result as \(W(k,r)\ge \beta r^k \). If they  got that wrong, I wonder what else they got wrong.  But I will assume their proof is correct.

The lower and upper bounds are still in different zip codes, but at least now they can send each other postcards.

-----------------------------------
4) Let \(g_d(n)\) be the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an \(n\)-point set in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).  Erdős made two conjectures about \(g_d(n)\).

CONJECTURE ONE:
\(g_2(n)=\Omega(n/\sqrt{\log n}) \). This matches the upper bound achieved by the points in a \(\sqrt{n} \times \sqrt{n}\) grid.  Guth and Katz showed in 2010 that \(g_2(n)=\Omega(n/\log n) \).

CONJECTURE TWO:
What happens for general \(d\)?

Erdős proved that, for all \(d\ge 3\), \(g_d(n) = O(n^{2/d})\).

Erdős conjectured that, for all  \(d\ge 3\), \(g_d(n) = \Theta(n^{2/d})\).

In 2008, Solymosi and Vu proved that, for all \(d\ge 4\), \(g_d(n)=\Omega(n^{2/d-2/(d(d+2))})\), and \(g_3(n)=\Omega(n^{0.5643})\).

OPENAI PROVED CONJECTURE TWO

There had been improvements in low dimensions since then, most notably Tidor, Yu, and Zakharov's proof that \(g_3(n)\ge n^{2/3-o(1)}\), but the conjecture remained open for general \(d\).

OpenAI showed that, for all \(d\ge 3\), \(g_d(n)=\Omega(n^{2/d})\).

So now we know that, for all \(d\ge 3\), \(g_d(n)=\Theta(n^{2/d})\).

Or do we? The result has not been Lean-formalized (as of October 9, 2026).

I wonder if OpenAI or Anthropic or some young scrappy upstart will close the small gap in the upper and lower bounds for \(g_2(n)\).

------------------------
5)  Hilbert's Tenth Problem over \(\mathbb{Q}\)

Hilbert's Tenth Problem over \(\mathbb{Z}\), the standard version, is the following decision problem:

Find an algorithm that will, given a polynomial \(p\in \mathbb{Z}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), determine whether there are integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in \mathbb{Z}\) such that \(p(a_1,\ldots,a_n)=0\).

Hilbert likely intended this problem to stimulate research in number theory.  It did to some extent. Davis-Putnam-Robinson and Matiyasevich showed the problem was undecidable. In my view, the proof used clever number theory but not deep number theory.

Since the problem over \(\mathbb{Z}\) is undecidable, it is natural to ask the question over other domains such as \(\mathbb{Q}\). For the domains \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(\mathbb{C}\) the problem is known to be decidable (see later in this entry). But for \(\mathbb{Q}\) it was open. If it is decidable
then that might lead to interesting number theory. (THANKS to a commenter who pointed out I should ask about other domains.) 


Here is the formulation:

Find an algorithm that will, given a polynomial \(p\in \mathbb{Z}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), determine whether there are rationals  \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in \mathbb{Q}\) such that \(p(a_1,\ldots,a_n)=0\).

OpenAI showed that this problem is also undecidable. It has not been Lean-formalized.

Judging from the table of contents, the proof looks like it uses deep math.  So maybe the problem did lead to interesting number theory, as Hilbert would have wanted. 

A table of what is known over other domains is here.

--------------------------------------------
6) Is there a non-trivial automorphism of the Turing degrees?

Let TD be the set of all Turing degrees.
An automorphism of the Turing degrees is a bijection \(f\) from TD to TD such that

\( a \le_T b \) if and only if \( f(a) \le_T f(b) \).

A non-trivial automorphism is one that is not the identity function.

In the mid-1960s Hartley Rogers posed the question:

Are there any non-trivial automorphisms of TD?

Slaman and Woodin wrote an unpublished manuscript titled Definability in Degree Structures where they prove that the number of automorphisms of TD is countable. (The bibliography of the OpenAI article on this problem gives 2005 for the year.)

This is a hard manuscript to find (I can't find it---if you can then leave a comment). ADDED LATER: a commenter DID find it and left a comment. 

GOOD NEWS: the manuscript is here.

BAD NEWS: Now I don't have an excuse to not read it. 

ODD POINT: There are still times when asking a set of people is better than asking Google or even Google AI.

This is a hard manuscript to read (I've heard).

The manuscript uses models of set theory to prove results in recursion theory.

OpenAI showed that there are no non-trivial automorphisms of TD. Lean-formalized.

There are very few people working on this problem. It may take a while to get it human-understood.

link.title: Conjectures that I thought would not be proved in my lifetime....were

entry.title: Open No More
entry.content:
I wrote the post below last week. That was a quaint and quiet time. Last night OpenAI released a treasure trove of 722 manuscripts solving 372 major open problems in mathematics including from theoretical computer science:

  • A proof of the unique games conjecture (formalized in Lean)
  • A full derandomization of randomized log space
  • Matrix multiplication in \(n^{2.25+\epsilon}\) time (formalized in Lean)
And many many more. I had Claude put together a webpage to make it easier to explore the TCS-related results.

Now these proofs haven't been fully verified but if they hold up, we've seen more progress in theoretical computer science in the last 24 hours than in the previous three decades combined!

It will take a while to process all these results, and what it means to the field of theoretical computer science and those who work within it. Much more in future posts.

A few caveats. As incredibly impressive as this work is, AI isn't solving everything--it solved under 10% of the problems given to it. And none of these results get us any closer to settling P v NP.

Nevertheless this will be a day we will never forget. Now on to my original post of far less important results.


Back in January, Matt Kovacs-Deak, Daochen Wang and Rain Zimin Yang solved my open question about the decision tree complexity of rational functions. With the help of AI some of my other open questions are continuing to get solved.

Adam Bouland, Andrew Huang, Anand Natarajan, Itay Shalit and Avishay Tal posted a paper giving an oracle where \(\mathrm{BQP}\) is not in \(\mathrm{IP}\) (interactive proofs). Now \(\mathrm{BQP}\) is in \(\mathrm{IP}\) since \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}=\mathrm{IP}\), but the \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) proof doesn't relativize and Bouland et al. show you can even get an oracle that puts \(\mathrm{BQP}\) out of \(\mathrm{IP}\).

The paper also states "Together with recent work due to Scott Aaronson, Anand Natarajan, Avishay Tal, and Ági Villányi, our work also gives the first oracle separation between IP and MIP, answering a question dating back to Fortnow's thesis." \(\mathrm{MIP}\) is the set of languages with multi-prover interactive proofs.

When I saw this paper, I pulled my PhD thesis off the shelf and indeed on page 40 I wrote "What is the relation between MIP and IP? Is there, for instance, an oracle separating the two classes".

When I wrote the thesis in 1989 we didn't know yet that \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) and \(\mathrm{MIP}=\mathrm{NEXP}\) so we really didn't have any idea whether multiple provers actually gave you more power than one prover. When László Babai, Carsten Lund and I proved \(\mathrm{MIP}=\mathrm{NEXP}\) a year later, we had strong evidence that \(\mathrm{IP}\neq\mathrm{MIP}\) since we believe that \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\neq\mathrm{NEXP}\). However since the proof that \(\mathrm{MIP}=\mathrm{NEXP}\) doesn't relativize either, the question of the oracle separation between \(\mathrm{IP}\) and \(\mathrm{MIP}\) remained open until the Bouland et al. paper.

Finally, Eshan Chattopadhyay, Pooya Hatami, Chin Ho Lee, Shachar Lovett, Avishay Tal and Emanuele Viola gave new exponential correlation bounds for polynomials. The authors use that bound to give a new pseudorandom generator against \(\mathrm{AC}^0[\oplus]\) circuits.

When I saw the paper I realized one could use this generator to show that \(\text{Almost-}\oplus\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}^{\oplus\mathrm{P}}\), answering a question I had wondered about in the 90s. Here \(\text{Almost-}\oplus\mathrm{P}\) is the class of languages \(L\) such that \(L\in\oplus\mathrm{P}^R\) with probability one for a random oracle \(R\). This in turn could be used to give an alternative proof of Toda's theorem. Ken Regan and Jim Royer showed that relative to a random oracle the polynomial-time hierarchy is contained in \(\oplus\mathrm{P}\), so \(\mathrm{PH}\subseteq\text{Almost-}\oplus\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}^{\oplus\mathrm{P}}\). It would take me a long time to work out and write up the details so I had Claude do it for me.

I still have many more open problems, see for example my survey of open oracle questions. I'd be happy to see them solved. Feel free to use AI but verify the proof. You too could get mentioned on this blog.

entry.title: How many humans does it take to make tech seem human? Do you want to be one of them?
entry.content:
(This was written about 9 months ago.  Its not out of date... yet)


People think that AI is going to DESTROY some jobs and CREATE some jobs. It may be too early to tell if this is true. Even so, here are some thoughts. 

1) Who will win? Who will lose?

2) Historically in the long term society was better off after a tech change (e.g., we live longer now than we did in the farm-era). Will that happen here as well?

3) We have some sense of what kinds of jobs will be destroyed. But what kind will be created? Will they be interesting? See later in this blog for a job you might not have thought of. 

4) Many jobs will change.  If you are over X years old then think about how much technology has changed your job even before the AI revolution. (The value of X may vary depending on how high-tech you are.) 

For an intelligent view of the questions above, see here.

For my view of one aspect of this, read on. 


There is one job which has been either created or expanded by AI:

Annotator.

(See here for an ARTICLE about these jobs, from which I got most of the rest of this post. The word ARTICLE is in caps so when I refer to it later you'll know what I am referring to.) 

The job consists of looking at pictures and labeling things.

Here is a direct quote from the manual: 

LABEL real items that can be worn by real people.

Does Lady Gaga count as a real person? She sometimes wears dresses made of meat. Should that count?  See here for a real article about her and see here for the Weird Al parody of Born that Way. Note that this is Weird AL, not Weird Artificial Intelligence. (See here for the Weird AI for Weird AL problem.)


They do this to create data for AI.

a) The jobs don't pay well though there are some exceptions.

b) The jobs are boring though there are some exceptions (and that may depend on the worker). 

c) This job is needed because AI keeps running into edge cases. This may have happened with AI's attempts to solve my GROUP ONE-GROUP TWO prez-VP problem from a prior blog post here  or my baseball-brother-pitchers post here.

c) KEY: People in AI used to think this is a temporary thing and these jobs will soon be automated. This might not  be the case. There are SO MANY edge cases that AI encounters. The more we expect from AI the more edge cases there will be.

A quote from page 26 (of the ARTICLE pointed to above) which is informative if you can parse it. I think. 

Put another way, ChatGPT seems so human because it was trained by an AI that was mimicking humans who were rating an AI that was mimicking humans who were pretending to be a better version of an AI that was trained on human writing.

entry.title: Does Programming Help You Understand Complexity?
entry.content:
I got the following question in an email.

My nephew is currently in high school in China and has developed a strong interest in computer science and mathematics. Recently, we've been talking about how computers can solve incredibly complex problems, yet there are still some problems that even the most powerful computers struggle to handle efficiently. I work in backend data maintenance myself, so I often think about how much a system's performance depends on the way a problem is approached, rather than simply how powerful the technology is.

From your experience, what do you think is the most important thing a young student should understand about the limits of what computers can do? Would you encourage someone like my nephew to begin exploring these questions through mathematics and logical reasoning, or to start by writing programs and discovering the challenges through practice?

A great question with no perfect answer. For me, I did considerable programming in high school and college in the early days of personal computers. Computers were slow so you really had to optimize. I learned new algorithmic techniques mostly from talking to other programmers and there were some problems that the computers just didn't have enough time to solve. Those experiences definitely helped me have a good understanding of the power of good algorithms and the limitations of computing when I later went into theoretical computer science.

But many of my colleagues successfully went into the field from the mathematical side without much programming experience and did fine. 

My experience comes from a different time. Now computers are much faster and AI can just give you the best known algorithms. We have much better algorithms for NP-complete problems like Satisfiability. Unless you go looking for hard problems, you'll rarely hit one you can't solve.

Reminds me of when I took my daughter driving during a snow storm to teach her how to handle a skid. In an empty parking lot I told her to move fast and hit hard on the brakes. The car just stopped. She failed to learn because of anti-lock brakes.

Ultimately, to learn why some problems are hard, you need to understand some theoretical computer science, particularly why the halting problem is impossible to solve and why NP-complete problems are likely hard. How you get there depends on the person.

If your nephew likes to program, you can give him the challenge of trying to solve some SAT competition problems or solving some of the hard LeetCode problems. If he is more into mathematics, ask him to try to come up with a SAT algorithm mathematically so he understands how hard the problem is. The difference today is that you have to search out hard problems as it's just less likely to run into them naturally.
